body.text: Port Vila, Vanuatu’s traffic-clogged yet charming capital city, is aflutter with flags in the week I visit. They are high up in trees, poking out of women’s hair, shading entrances to restaurants, pinned to the walls of many of the city’s large number of kava bars. They bedeck the minibuses helping jam the traffic, some of them financed by years spent in Australia on seasonal-worker programs.

About half the flags are Vanuatu’s, with its Y-shaped red, yellow, green and black ensemble and rounded pig tusk encircling two cycad leaves. Its ubiquity makes sense, my visit coinciding with a week of celebrations for the country’s forty-sixth Independence Day. But the sheer range of other flags flying in the city doesn’t make immediate sense. A few are from Argentina and Brazil, some Dutch, a handful Belgian, all of which are outnumbered by those of England and France.

Why that pair of flags? Filled with historical factoids from having read many traveller’s tales of Vanuatu — or the New Hebrides, as it was known before independence — I wonder whether they are signalling the two countries’ almost comically dire and frequently quarrelsome joint rule over this island archipelago during most of the twentieth century.

Officially called a condominium, the British–French administration of the New Hebrides was dubbed by passing journalists “the pandemonium” because Britain and France could agree to almost nothing. Alexander Frater, a gifted Port Vila–born travel writer, described the chaos: “two flags, two anthems, two sets of postage stamps, two police forces, two legal systems…”

The lengths to which the British and French went to undermine each other went right down to the selection of the ultimate arbiter of law in the colony, a Spanish judge who spoke neither good English nor good French. Of the two jails, the French served better food. Of the two hospitals, Frater averred the British was best, but then his father was the doctor.

And if those flags were ubiquitous, some of the here-and-now powers trying to shape the modern Pacific were notably absent. Few of the ensigns belonged to either Australia or China, the two countries locked in a diplomatic arm-wrestle for favour in this island nation. Indeed, Australia’s slim lead over China’s tally was probably equal to the number of Colombian ensigns.

I felt foolish when I realised I was missing the most obvious explanation. The other flags and their prominence had nothing to do with geopolitical posturing or a hearkening back to old rule and everything to do with the World Cup, which had recently concluded. England and France both reached the semi-finals; China didn’t qualify at all; the Australian team whimpered out early.

The fact I was primed to see significances that didn’t exist says much about Port Vila, a place that gets more attention these days than it once did, almost of all of it geopolitics-related. Type Vanuatu into Google and back come so many stories about Australia and China competing for influence that they conjure images of a Checkpoint Charlie in the tropics. Often the stories are not written from Port Vila at all but from Canberra or Washington, sometimes padded out with commentary from analysts who have spent varying amounts of time in the country. The reporting has the feel of sports statistics, focusing on the number of agreements signed, kit donated, buildings opened.

Maybe the hype of the foreign correspondent was ever thus. In his book The Coconut War Richard Shears, an Australian journalist who covered a shortlived uprising in Vanuatu’s northern islands during its independence year of 1980, recounts a conversation with his editor upon his arrival in Port Vila. Unhappy with Shears’s observation that the most noteworthy thing about Port Vila was its torpor, the editor told him other correspondents had filed more captivating pieces under headlines like “War Chants in Paradise.” Shears disappointed the unhappy fellow by telling him those pieces were all filed from London, adding that the only flowing blood he had found was oozing out of planters’ beefsteaks.

Shears’s lively book is also a story about the importance of going to see a place for yourself. Although his reportage is largely forgotten, his advice remains true and I had decided to take it. I thought I would try to take the measure of what was really happening in Port Vila and seek out some of the places that had been generating so much attention.

On previous visits to Vanuatu I’d been working as an aid consultant on assignments that left little time for moseying around, and under various degrees of subtle pressure to ensure certain lines are toed. It felt liberating to be off the leash.

My plan was to park my hire car somewhere in the compact city centre, start walking and see what I could find. I found a park next to mound of rubble fenced off from the street, remnant of those large parts of Port Vila’s CBD devastated during the Christmas 2024 earthquake that killed fourteen people. Parts of the city are being rebuilt but large sections resemble a demolition site. It’s a reminder that the biggest threat to Vanuatu’s stability might come not from faraway countries but from tectonic plates. Port Vila sits directly atop the “ring of fire,” making it one of the most earthquake-prone cities in the world.

Certainly, there are enough signs in the city centre to provoke apoplexy among Australia’s China hawks. I walk past Churchill House — named for the British PM who, as under-secretary of state for the colonies, helped usher in the British–French compromise arrangements in 1907 — and find it is now home to a Chinese bank, Wanfuteng, registered in Hong Kong to serve the Vanuatu market. On either side of the building and across the street are a bunch of Chinese-run stores selling Vanuatu-themed t-shirts, bags, wristbands and hats. Their prime clientele are the Australian tourists who roam the city on a day’s pass from the cruise ships.

A little further on is a fenced-off construction site, with building works well advanced, displaying a prominent “China Aid” sign. This is one among many signs displaying those two words throughout the city. Beijing is rebuilding government buildings — the artist’s impression on the hoardings is lavish and imposing — and familiar old institutions, too, are becoming Chinese owned, as some Vila old-timers had lamented to me. Among them is L’Houstalet, the French restaurant where Vanuatu’s independence constitution was finalised over onion soup. (The original document even has some telltale stains on it.) One of the most quintessentially French places in the tropics, it was recently sold to new Chinese owners.

I turn up a flight of steep stairs which takes me past the Australian High Commission on Winston Churchill Avenue, another nod to the former British leader. It strikes me again that he is a strange choice for such prodigious naming. He never visited this corner of the Empire and one of his few public statements on the islands was to describe it as a “place of cannibalism and other savage customs [where] a state of disorder has always prevailed.” No matter the era, the major powers of the day have always imagined the islands in a way that suits their own interests.

The High Commission, a low-slung, dun-coloured building with a no-nonsense metal gate, is dwarfed by a monstrous carbuncle — a giant convention centre marked also by hoardings showing a Chinese flag. Its exterior looks intact, but parts of the interior are collapsing inwards; it was falling into disrepair even before the earthquake fatally damaged it.

Matt Francis, a writer of cosy crime novels about Vanuatu under a pseudonym designed to avoid strife in this small, networked country, described how anyone seeking to hire the centre had to pay for a clean-up not only after but also before any event because the empty hall constantly gathered dust. “Even worse,” he added, “[they] were told to bring their own toilet paper.”

A little further down Winston Churchill Avenue, Independence Park is being spruced up for the celebrations. The noonday sun is getting hot. A shaded viewing area has largely been repainted, and a few people sleeping on the concrete seats spring up, paintbrushes in hand, when they see me approaching. One man sheepishly tells me he thought I was there to check on progress. In truth, I wanted to have a closer look at the two flag poles of equal height just in front of the stand. On this spot, British and French flags once flew: the meticulous attention the colonial administrations paid to ensuring their even height was a time-honoured observation of passing journalists.

A palpable sense of pride and anticipation is in the air. The significant number of people milling around Independence Park are decked out in vibrant t-shirts in the colours of the national flag, and stallholders are laying out carvings, flags and pictures. National pride is a hard emotion to gauge accurately, but it feels palpable on this muggy afternoon, reminiscent of the mood that prevails on Timor-Leste’s Independence Day but unlike in Solomon Islands, Vanuatu’s northern neighbour, where I’ve found the celebrations to be muted, nondescript, forced affairs.

My likening of Vanuatu to Timor-Leste is not entirely misplaced, Ben Bohane tells me when I call in for a visit that comes with the added benefit of respite from the heat. Bohane is a war photographer, journalist and television producer who has made Port Vila home and is now a Vanuatu citizen. (Check out his amazing book, The Black Islands, which is available on his website.) He lives in an old colonial house filled with mementoes acquired during more than thirty years of reporting the region, along with one of the finest collections of old books about the Pacific.

We talk about differences between Vanuatu’s independence story and the experience in many other parts of the Pacific, where colonial powers Australia and Britain couldn’t get shot of their possessions fast enough. Independence for Vanuatu was more fraught. France didn’t want to relinquish control and was egging on a movement in the country’s north that was unhappy that the country-to-be’s elected leaders were more of an anglophone than a francophone bent.

Vanuatu’s independence leaders learnt to play off the French and British during the colonial period, he said, which may have equipped them to play off China and Australia in the current era. He described the country as the Switzerland of the Pacific, the only genuinely independent republic in the region.

Vanuatu’s leaders have long had a strong independent streak and this makes them unusual in the club of nations, which tends to be sniffy about new members wanting to join. Vanuatu was pretty much on its own in backing Timor-Leste’s struggle for independence from Indonesia and has long supported West Papuan independence too.

I leave Bohane and walk up a vertiginous hill, thinking about how adroitly the Vanuatu government is navigating the region’s geopolitics and how much it is enjoying its place in the sun. During a previous work assignment I had met a senior police officer who was luxuriating in the benefits of all the competition. “If the Australians don’t give me what I ask then I say I’ll go to China and then they give me what I want,” he told me. “And vice versa,” he added with studied equanimity and a smile.

Going on the look of the Vanuatu Police Force, the gambit is working a treat. A speedway’s worth of police motorcycles roar past me up the hill, each bearing the mark of something called the Vanuatu Australia Policing and Justice Partnership, a mildly Orwellian appellation signalling an equivalence that obscures the fact that Canberra provides all the money for it to continue. Two wheels good, four wheels better? There seem to be just as many police cars as bikes.

It’s not just vehicles. Australia is investing big in Vanuatu’s security sector. A giant new police station is being built in the city’s Georges Pompidou area. Close by is Cook barracks, named for the captain and home to Vanuatu’s perennially underemployed Mobile Force, a paramilitary arm of the police. I visited the barracks a few times about a decade or so ago when it consisted of little more than a few ramshackle prefabs accessible by walking underneath a rusted boom gate pointing to the skies in a half-hearted military salute. Inside I’d encountered a few police marching up and down in desultory fashion, waiting as if for an order that would never come.

There’s no chance of a bimble around the new barracks now, refurbished to the tune of A$60 million, or the equivalent of just under a tenth of the country’s annual budget. It is a much sturdier looking construction although I can’t help wondering if the paramilitary police have much more to do in this most peaceable of cities. When I walked around the previous evening the only possible danger I encountered was a few unexpected potholes; I could never have walked around that other Pacific “Port” — Port Moresby — of an evening (or even during the day) in such cavalier fashion. Vanuatu, I read, ranks 186th out of 193 on the Global Organised Crime Index. (Australia is 152nd.)

I walk down the hill, past the present modest-sized police HQ. Next door, I notice, is a new Chinese Christian church. It seems like the sort of absurdist coincidence that could be a plotline in the next Matt Francis novel.

With the sun well over the yard-arm I’m heading for a beer in an old haunt from assignments past. It’s in an idyllic location, looking out onto tall sailing yachts anchored in the lagoon and the palm trees swaying on Iririki island, once a home for missionaries and British colonial officers. Now it’s a hotel popular with Australian schoolies, a bit of a step down from its heyday when topee-hatted butlers welcomed the likes of Bryan Ferry and Steven Spielberg. It is also where Alexander Frater, author of the book under my arm, was born.

My only companions in the bar this early, balmy evening are yachties. The geopolitical storms swirling around Vanuatu feel a long way away as I read Frater describing his return to Iririki, where he found that all the buildings from his childhood — all the half-hearted efforts of the colonial administration to put down permanent markers — are decaying or gone. All that remained on the island was what he characterised as a sterile resort.
Frater himself is long dead but his words are a reminder that nothing the outside powers try to do to Vanuatu is permanent, except maybe the street names. •
